title: Finding Unclaimed Retirement Benefits of the Deceased (October 2026)
summary: Find unclaimed retirement benefits left by a deceased person using free national and state databases. Guide updated October 2026.
body_markdown:
Retirement accounts, pensions, and survivor benefits left by a deceased person can sit unclaimed across multiple separate registries. There is no single database that covers all account types at once, which is why locating them generally takes more than one search. This article covers: what types of retirement benefits can go unclaimed, where and how to search different registries, what beneficiary designations control, how to use old financial documents as a starting point, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Roughly 31.9 million forgotten retirement accounts hold an estimated $2.1 trillion in assets across multiple separate registries
- Beneficiary forms on retirement accounts override a will, so outdated designations can redirect funds or stall a claim entirely
- Non-spouse beneficiaries who inherit an IRA or 401(k) face a 10-year withdrawal window under SECURE Act 2.0, with a 25% penalty for missed distributions
- Tax returns and Social Security earnings records are reliable starting points for locating accounts when no financial records exist
- Elayne's Financial Discovery tier scans tax returns, bank statements, and financial records to surface retirement accounts, survivor benefits, and unclaimed state property in one structured search


## What Types of Retirement Benefits Can Go Unclaimed


Several distinct categories of[retirement benefits after a death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/discovering-401-k-and-retirement-benefits-after-a-death) can sit unclaimed. Examples include:


Benefit Type Typical Holder


401(k) / 403(b) Former employer's plan administrator


Defined-benefit pension Employer or PBGC (if plan terminated)


Traditional / Roth IRA Bank, brokerage, or credit union


Government / military pension Federal, state, or local agency


Social Security survivor benefits Social Security Administration


Veterans' benefits Department of Veterans Affairs


## How Beneficiary Designations Affect What You Can Claim


Beneficiary designations on retirement accounts work independently of a will. Whatever name appears on the account's beneficiary form is who receives the funds, regardless of what the deceased's will says.


Outdated designations can create real complications. A form completed 20 years ago, before a divorce or remarriage, can route assets to an ex-spouse. A form naming a beneficiary who has since died can stall the claim entirely. Other key points to note include:


- If the beneficiary designation is blank or was never completed, the funds typically pass to the estate, go through probate, and take longer to reach heirs.
- If the named beneficiary is a minor child, a court-appointed guardian may need to manage the funds until the child reaches adulthood.
- Some plans allow contingent beneficiaries who inherit only if the primary beneficiary has died; if neither designation is updated, fallback rules vary by plan.

## The National Registry of Unclaimed Retirement Benefits


The National Registry of Unclaimed Retirement Benefits is a free, searchable database powered by PenChecks Trust. Employers voluntarily list accounts of former employees they have lost track of, making it a practical starting point for beneficiaries searching on behalf of someone who has died.


A search requires only a Social Security number. If a match appears, a former employer or plan custodian has registered that person as having unclaimed funds. The beneficiary then contacts the plan administrator or PenChecks Trust directly to initiate a claim or rollover. The registry does not hold the funds in every case; some employers retain the account and use the registry only to locate the participant.


## The DOL's Retirement Savings Lost and Found Database


The DOL's Retirement Savings Lost and Found Database was created under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 as a centralized, free resource where former employees and their beneficiaries can search private-sector retirement plans. A Login.gov account with identity verification is required to search.


As of this writing, the database is limited to those 65 and older, narrowing its usefulness for beneficiaries of younger account holders. The DOL has indicated the scope may expand over time, so checking the DOL's Lost and Found page directly will reflect the current eligibility criteria. Plan sponsor participation is also voluntary, so not every private-sector plan appears in results.


## How to Search the PBGC for a Lost Pension


The[PBGC's unclaimed retirement benefits database](https://www.pbgc.gov/workers-retirees/find-unclaimed-retirement-benefits/search-unclaimed) holds funds transferred from private-sector pension plans that ended and could not locate their participants. If the deceased worked for a company that shut down or terminated its pension plan, their benefits may have been transferred to PBGC for safekeeping.


Searching requires only a last name and the last four digits of a Social Security number. The database is updated quarterly. A match means PBGC is holding funds on behalf of that person, and a beneficiary can then apply to claim them.


## The DOL's Abandoned Plan Database


The[DOL's Abandoned Plan Search](https://www.askebsa.dol.gov/abandonedplansearch/) serves a different purpose than the Lost and Found database. When an employer stops operating and can no longer maintain a retirement plan, the DOL's Abandoned Plan Program steps in to wind it down and distribute benefits to participants. A Qualified Termination Administrator (QTA) takes over and manages that process.


The search is free and requires no account. Entering the former employer's name or the plan name is enough to check whether a plan is in termination and who the QTA is. No Social Security number is needed to run the initial search, though the QTA will require identity documentation (typically a government-issued ID and a certified death certificate) before releasing any funds. Once a QTA is identified, contacting them directly is the right starting point for filing a claim. Timelines vary depending on where the plan is in the wind-down process; a plan in early termination may take longer to distribute than one already in final stages.


## What to Do When the Former Employer No Longer Exists


When a former employer no longer exists, the pension or 401(k) doesn't automatically disappear. The plan assets had to go somewhere, and tracing them takes a few targeted steps.


- State corporate registries often show whether a company was acquired, merged, or dissolved, and by whom, which can support a broader effort to[find financial accounts after someone dies](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-find-all-bank-and-investment-accounts-after-someone-dies) .
- Form 5500 filings, searchable through the DOL's EFAST2 system, are annual reports every ERISA plan must file; they name the plan administrator, trustee, and insurance carrier even after a company closes.
- If the plan had an insurance carrier backing it, that carrier may still hold the funds or can direct you to whoever does.
- The DOL's Abandoned Plan Database shows whether a terminated plan entered the Abandoned Plan Program and which QTA is managing the wind-down.


If a company was acquired, the acquiring company often assumed responsibility for the pension or retirement plan. Reaching out to that company's HR or benefits department is one way to[find hidden accounts after death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-find-hidden-accounts-after-death) that might otherwise go unnoticed.

## FAQ


### How do I search for unclaimed retirement benefits of a deceased person across multiple systems?


The National Registry of Unclaimed Retirement Benefits, the DOL's Retirement Savings Lost and Found database, and the PBGC's unclaimed pension database each cover a different category of plan and are practical starting points. The deceased's tax returns, including W-2s and 1099-Rs, name the specific institutions that held accounts. State unclaimed property databases are a valuable resource as well.


### What happens to a 401(k) or inherited IRA if no beneficiary was named?


When no beneficiary designation exists, the account typically passes to the estate, goes through probate, and takes longer to reach heirs. The more favorable inherited IRA distribution rules under SECURE Act 2.0 (including the option to roll funds into an inherited IRA) often do not apply in this scenario, which can increase the income tax burden on distributions.


### Can I find a deceased parent's lost pension if their former employer no longer exists?


The DOL's Abandoned Plan database shows whether a terminated plan entered the Abandoned Plan Program and names the Qualified Termination Administrator managing the wind-down. Form 5500 filings, searchable through the DOL's EFAST2 system, list the plan administrator and trustee even after a company closes. If the company was acquired, the acquiring company often assumed responsibility for the retirement plan.


### What are the SECURE Act 2.0 distribution rules for an inherited IRA in 2026?


Most non-spouse beneficiaries face a 10-year window to withdraw all funds, and starting in 2026, mandatory annual RMDs are required within that window; missing a distribution carries a 25% penalty on the amount that should have been taken. Surviving spouses have more flexibility: they can roll the inherited account into their own IRA, defer distributions based on their own age, and avoid the 10-year rule entirely. Minor children, disabled individuals, and those less than 10 years younger than the deceased qualify for extended treatment.
